claims.claim: CAV1 KO mice show higher lethality when subjected to a catalytically active mART exotoxin targeting RhoA during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
claims.source: Consistent with the increase in TEM density and width in siCAV1 cells, we record a higher lethality in CAV1 KO mice subjected to a catalytically active mART exotoxin targeting RhoA during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5 comparing Cav1-/- and Cav1+/+ mice infected with S. aureus strains.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 contributes to membrane stiffening in addition to the role of cavin-1/caveolin-1-dependent caveolae in the control of membrane tension homeostasis.
claims.source: Combined theoretical modeling with independent biophysical measurements of plasma membrane bending rigidity points toward a specific contribution of caveolin-1 to membrane stiffening in addition to the role of cavin-1/caveolin-1-dependent caveolae in the control of membrane tension homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D and theoretical modeling described in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: The endothelial cell monolayer lining the inner surface of the vascular tree forms an active semipermeable barrier that actively responds to hemodynamic forces to control blood pressure.
claims.source: The endothelial cell monolayer lining the inner surface of the vascular tree forms an active semipermeable barrier that actively responds to hemodynamic forces to control blood pressure (Aird, 2007a; Aird, 2007b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aird, 2007a and Aird, 2007b.

claims.claim: Regulation of the endothelial barrier involves a bidirectional interplay between actomyosin cytoskeleton and plasma membrane mechanics.
claims.source: Regulation of the endothelial barrier involves a bidirectional interplay between actomyosin cytoskeleton and plasma membrane mechanics, which together control paracellular exchanges at cell–cell junctions (Komarova et al., 2017), as well as transcellular exchanges through less-characterized transcellular openings (Aird, 2007a; Aird, 2007b; Guo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Komarova et al., 2017, Aird, 2007a, Aird, 2007b, and Guo et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition.
claims.source: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins, which catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition, induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, and Maddugoda et al., 2011.

claims.claim: mART exotoxins induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter.
claims.source: Bacterial mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART) exotoxins, which catalyze the post-translational modification of the small GTPase RhoA for inhibition, induce the spontaneous formation of transendothelial cell macroaperture (TEM) tunnels up to 10–20 µm in diameter (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, and Maddugoda et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The mART group includes the exotoxin C3 (ExoC3) from Clostridium botulinum and the epidermal differentiation inhibitors (EDIN) A, B, and C close homologs from Staphylococcus aureus.
claims.source: This group of mART includes the exotoxin C3 (ExoC3) from Clostridium botulinum and the epidermal differentiation inhibitors (EDIN) A, B, and C close homologs from Staphylococcus aureus (Sugai et al., 1992; Chardin et al., 1989; Paterson et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sugai et al., 1992, Chardin et al., 1989, and Paterson et al., 1990.

claims.claim: The intravenous injection of EDIN or ExoC3 triggers vascular leakage.
claims.source: The intravenous injection of EDIN or ExoC3 triggers vascular leakage (Boyer et al., 2006; Rolando et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Rolando et al., 2009.

claims.claim: EDIN favors the translocation of S. aureus through vascular tissues for dissemination.
claims.source: Cumulative evidence also indicates that EDIN favors the translocation of S. aureus through vascular tissues for dissemination (Munro et al., 2010; Courjon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Munro et al., 2010 and Courjon et al., 2015.

claims.claim: TEM tunnels form ex vivo in the endothelium lining the inner surface of rat aortas either infected with S. aureus producing the RhoA-targeting EDIN mART or treated with EDIN.
claims.source: Although TEM tunnels have not yet been visualized in vivo, they form ex vivo in the endothelium lining the inner surface of rat aortas either infected with S. aureus producing the RhoA-targeting EDIN mART or treated with EDIN (Boyer et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boyer et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The inhibition of RhoA signaling by bacterial mART exotoxins disrupts contractile actomyosin stress fibers.
claims.source: Mechanistically, the inhibition of RhoA signaling by bacterial mART exotoxins disrupts contractile actomyosin stress fibers, which otherwise stiffen in response to shear forces exerted by the blood flow that tends to compress cells (Boyer et al., 2006; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020; Maddugoda et al., 2011; Sugai et al., 1992; Chardin et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2020, Maddugoda et al., 2011, Sugai et al., 1992, and Chardin et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Compressive mechanical forces applied to the apical region of endothelial cells bring into close contact the apical and basal plasma membranes to nucleate transcellular pores.
claims.source: In line with this, compressive mechanical forces applied to the apical region of endothelial cells bring into close contact the apical and basal plasma membranes to nucleate transcellular pores (Ng et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the force required to mechanically open TEMs dramatically decreases when RhoA is inhibited.
claims.source: Although force-induced nucleation of TEMs can be triggered in the absence of inhibition of RhoA, the magnitude of the force required to mechanically open TEMs dramatically decreases when RhoA is inhibited (Ng et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ng et al., 2017.

claims.claim: TEMs form because of a disruption of actomyosin stress fibers under the control of RhoA, which concur to reduce the height of cells as they spread out.
claims.source: This led to postulate that TEMs form because of a disruption of actomyosin stress fibers under the control of RhoA, which concur to reduce the height of cells as they spread out (Boyer et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2006 and Tsai et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The increase in membrane tension in response to cell spreading is the driving force of TEM nucleation.
claims.source: Notably, the analogy drawn between liquid and cellular dewetting suggests that the increase in membrane tension in response to cell spreading is the driving force of TEM nucleation also contributing to define the initial speed of opening, that is, before that membrane tension relaxation around TEM edges and build-up of an actomyosin bundle encircling TEMs counteract the opening (Maddugoda et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012; Stefani et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maddugoda et al., 2011, Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al., 2012, and Stefani et al., 2017, and represents a theoretical inference from the dewetting model.

claims.claim: Membrane bending rigidity contributes to TEM dynamics due to the high curvature of the plasma membrane at the edge of TEMs.
claims.source: Of note, the high curvature of the plasma membrane at the edge of TEMs also points toward a contribution of membrane bending rigidity, that is, the energy required to locally bend the membrane surface, in their dynamics.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed high curvature at TEM edges.

claims.claim: Caveolae are mechano-regulators of the plasma membrane that spontaneously flatten to accommodate acute mechanical loads and thereby prevent membrane rupturing.
claims.source: Caveolae are mechano-regulators of the plasma membrane that spontaneously flatten to accommodate acute mechanical loads and thereby prevent membrane rupturing (Sinha et al., 2011; Parton et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sinha et al., 2011 and Parton et al., 2020a.

claims.claim: Caveolin oligomers are essential components of caveolae pits.
claims.source: Caveolin oligomers are essential components of caveolae pits (Parton et al., 2006; Porta et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parton et al., 2006 and Porta et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 homo-oligomers form flat discoid complexes embedded into the inner leaflet of the membrane.
claims.source: Caveolin-1 homo-oligomers form flat discoid complexes embedded into the inner leaflet of the membrane (Porta et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Porta et al., 2022.

claims.claim: The process of invagination of caveolar pits of 50–100 nm diameter involves the association of caveolin-1 with cavin-1 cytosolic structural protein.
claims.source: The process of invagination of caveolar pits of 50–100 nm diameter involves the association of caveolin-1 with cavin-1 cytosolic structural protein (also referred to as PTRF) (Ludwig et al., 2013; Ariotti et al., 2015; Ludwig et al., 2016; Yang and Scarlata, 2017; Lamaze et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ludwig et al., 2013, Ariotti et al., 2015, Ludwig et al., 2016, Yang and Scarlata, 2017, and Lamaze et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Caveolae pits are stabilized at their neck by the assembly of a ring of dynamin-like EHD2 oligomers.
claims.source: Caveolae pits are further stabilized at their neck by the assembly of a ring of dynamin-like EHD2 oligomers (Daumke et al., 2007; Yeow et al., 2017; Nishimura and Suetsugu, 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Daumke et al., 2007, Yeow et al., 2017, and Nishimura and Suetsugu, 2022.

claims.claim: In endothelial cells, the crosstalk between caveolin-1 and RhoA during actomyosin contractility leads to critical mechano-sensing and adaptation to hemodynamic forces.
claims.source: In endothelial cells, the crosstalk between caveolin-1 and RhoA during actomyosin contractility leads to critical mechano-sensing and adaptation to hemodynamic forces (Yu et al., 2006; Del Pozo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2006 and Del Pozo et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1-deficient mice undergo an increase in the endothelial nitric oxide (eNOS) signaling that is critical to activate RhoA signaling via nitration-mediated inhibition of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of p190RhoGAP-A.
claims.source: For example, caveolin-1-deficient mice undergo an increase in the endothelial nitric oxide (eNOS) signaling that is critical to activate RhoA signaling via nitration-mediated inhibition of the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) activity of p190RhoGAP-A (Siddiqui et al., 2011; Razani et al., 2001; Miyawaki-Shimizu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Siddiqui et al., 2011, Razani et al., 2001, and Miyawaki-Shimizu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: ExoC3 treatment reduces the density of invaginated caveolae at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold.
claims.source: We recorded a 1.6-fold decrease in the mean density of caveolae in the ExoC3-treated cells, which exhibited 3.4 ± 2.1 caveolae/µm2 of membrane, compared to 5.4 ± 3.1 caveolae/µm2 of membrane in untreated cells (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The pool of plasma membrane-located caveolae remaining in ExoC3-treated cells is evenly distributed with no detectable accumulation around TEM tunnels.
claims.source: The pool of plasma membrane-located caveolae remaining in ExoC3-treated cells is evenly distributed with no detectable accumulation around TEM tunnels (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: siRNA-mediated depletion of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) strongly reduces both caveolin-1 and the cellular pool of cavin-1/PTRF by approximately 80%.
claims.source: We observed that small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated depletion of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) strongly reduces both caveolin-1 and the cellular pool of cavin-1/PTRF by approximately 80% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: About one-half of the pool of caveolin-1 remained unaffected by the siRNA-targeted depletion of cavin-1/PTRF (siPRTF).
claims.source: In contrast, about one-half of the pool of caveolin-1 remained unaffected by the siRNA-targeted depletion of cavin-1/PTRF (siPRTF) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both siRNA treatments (siCAV1 and siPTRF) had no effect on the extent of mono-ADPribosylation of RhoA.
claims.source: Both siRNA treatments had no effect on the extent of mono-ADPribosylation of RhoA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: A higher percentage of cells display at least one TEM in the population of caveolin-1 or cavin-1-deficient cells (37.6 ± 1.3% siCAV1 and 36.4 ± 1.3% siPTRF vs. 28.8 ± 1.2% siCTRL).
claims.source: Quantitative measurements showed a higher percentage of cells displaying at least one TEM in the population of caveolin-1 or cavin-1-deficient cells (37.6 ± 1.3% siCAV1 and 36.4 ± 1.3% siPTRF vs. 28.8 ± 1.2% siCTRL) (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: There is a significant increase in the density of TEMs per cell in siCAV1 (NTEM_siCAV1 = 1.96) and siPTRF (NTEM_siPTRF = 1.36) conditions compared to siCTRL (NsiCTRL = 0.91).
claims.source: Moreover, we observed a significant increase in the density of TEMs per cell in siCAV1 (NTEM_siCAV1 = 1.96) and siPTRF (NTEM_siPTRF = 1.36) conditions compared to siCTRL (NsiCTRL = 0.91) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The efficiency of the formation of TEMs is inversely correlated to the density and stability of caveolae at the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Together, these data show that the efficiency of the formation of TEMs is inversely correlated to the density and stability of caveolae at the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing increased TEM formation with caveolae depletion.

claims.claim: ExoC3 treatment induces a significant increase in actin mesh size of about 0.2 μm2 compared to non-intoxicated cells.
claims.source: In all conditions of siRNA treatment, we have measured that ExoC3 treatment induces a significant increase in actin mesh size of about 0.2 μm2 compared to non-intoxicated cells (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 2D STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: No significant difference of mesh size was recorded between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions before and after treatment with ExoC3.
claims.source: No significant difference of mesh size was recorded between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions before and after treatment with ExoC3 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 2D STORM imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: RhoA inhibition generates a loose F-actin meshwork framing large cellular zones devoid of F-actin of same extent in all siRNA conditions.
claims.source: We concluded that in addition to the well-established impact of RhoA inhibition on actin stress fibers it generates a loose F-actin meshwork framing large cellular zones devoid of F-actin of same extent in all siRNA conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on 2D STORM imaging observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Upon intoxication of siCTRL-treated cells, there is a significant increase of 36% of the spreading area together with 17% increase of the cell volume.
claims.source: Upon intoxication of siCTRL-treated cells, we recorded a significant increase of 36% of the spreading area together with 17% increase of the cell volume (Figure 3C and D and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D and Table 1.

claims.claim: The dominant impact of cell area changes over the volume parameter accounts for the calculated decrease of cell height of 15% in siCTRL-treated cells upon ExoC3 intoxication.
claims.source: The dominant impact of cell area changes over the volume parameter accounts for the calculated decrease of cell height of 15% (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on calculations from measured cell area and volume data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: When siCAV1- and siPTRF-transfected cells were treated with ExoC3, there is a reduction in cell volume concomitant to the increase in their spreading area.
claims.source: Hence, when siCAV1- and siPTRF-transfected cells were treated with ExoC3, we recorded a reduction in cell volume concomitant to the increase in their spreading area (Figure 3C and D and Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D and Table 1.

claims.claim: The reinforced reduction in cell height recorded in siCAV1 or siPTRF-treated cells is in good agreement with findings showing that these treatments increase the density of TEMs.
claims.source: The reinforced reduction in cell height recorded in siCAV1 or siPTRF-treated cells is in good agreement with our findings showing that these treatments increase the density of TEMs.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference connecting cell height measurements with TEM density observations.

claims.claim: In the absence of ExoC3, the effects of siPTRF on cell shape parameters were slightly stronger than those of siCAV1.
claims.source: Note that in the absence of ExoC3 we recorded that the effects of siPTRF on cell shape parameters were slightly stronger than those of siCAV1, thereby highlighting the key involvement of caveolae in the control of cell height (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The depletion of caveolae and the inhibition of RhoA work together to reduce cell height that favors together with the loss of F-actin the nucleation of TEMs.
claims.source: The depletion of caveolae and the inhibition of RhoA work together to reduce cell height that favors together with the loss of F-actin the nucleation of TEMs.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the combined effects of caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition on cell height and TEM formation.

claims.claim: TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1-treated cells compared to siPTRF- and siCTRL-treatments.
claims.source: Interestingly, we recorded 5.4-fold wider TEMs in siCAV1-treated cells compared to siPTRF- and siCTRL-treatments (Figure 4B and Videos 1–3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of maximal TEM areas shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The time for TEMs to reach their maximal diameter (tmax) and the overall TEM cycles (tc) remains identical in all conditions.
claims.source: Interestingly, the time for TEMs to reach their maximal diameter (tmax) and the overall TEM cycles (tc) remains identical in all conditions (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: There is a twofold higher opening speed in caveolin-1-depleted cells: So_siCAV1 = 2.4 µm2/s versus So_siCTRL = 1.1 µm2/s in control cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, we recorded a twofold higher opening speed in caveolin-1-depleted cells: So_siCAV1 = 2.4 µm2/s versus So_siCTRL = 1.1 µm2/s in control cells, which contrasts with the minor impact of siPTRF with So_siPTRF = 1.7 µm2/s (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by high temporal resolution imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 has a specific function in the regulation of the opening speed of TEMs that has a critical impact on TEM maximal width.
claims.source: In conclusion, we have identified a specific function of caveolin-1 in the regulation of the opening speed of TEMs that has a critical impact on TEM maximal width.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on TEM opening speeds and maximal widths.

claims.claim: The loss of caveolin-1 expression sensitizes mice to bloodstream infection triggered by S. aureus-produced EDIN-B.
claims.source: The loss of caveolin-1 expression thus sensitizes mice to bloodstream infection triggered by S. aureus-produced EDIN-B.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the survival data comparing Cav1-/- and Cav1+/+ mice.

claims.claim: When Cav1-/- mice were challenged with LD50 of S. aureus (2.5 × 10^7 CFU/m), there was lower survival with S. aureus WT edinB (n = 11 death/18 mice) compared to ΔedinB (n = 4 death/17 mice).
claims.source: When we challenged Cav1-/- mice with this LD50 of S. aureus (2.5 × 107 CFU/m), we saw a lower survival with S. aureus WT edinB (n = 11 death/18 mice) compared to ΔedinB (n = 4 death/17 mice) (p=0.0123, Mantel‒Cox test) (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: There is a significant decrease in survival in caveolin-1-deficient mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B compared to mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B-RE.
claims.source: We saw a significant decrease in survival in caveolin-1-deficient mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B compared to mice infected with ΔedinB pEDIN-B-RE.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data comparing mice infected with catalytically active versus inactive EDIN-B.

claims.claim: In the context of bloodstream infection by S. aureus, caveolin-1 expression confers a resistance to the pathogenicity triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA.
claims.source: We concluded that in the context of bloodstream infection by S. aureus, caveolin-1 expression confers a resistance to the pathogenicity triggered by EDIN-B mART activity on RhoA.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the survival experiments comparing wildtype and catalytically inactive EDIN-B.

claims.claim: Cells treated with siCAV1 have a significant twofold higher membrane tension than the controls.
claims.source: From our measurements, we deduce that cells treated with siCAV1 have a significant twofold higher membrane tension than the controls, and no effect in siPTRF-treated cells (see 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This claim is based on theoretical modeling and experimental measurements described in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: The model predicts a 55% reduction in membrane rigidity from a loss of expression of caveolin-1 and a lower reduction of 15% upon a loss of cavin-1 expression.
claims.source: Using the following values for the siCTRL-treated cells – an initial membrane tension σ0 = 2.5 10–5 N/m (Raucher and Sheetz, 2000) and a bending rigidity κsiCTRL = 23.4 kBT (direct measurement, see below) – the model predicts a 55% reduction in membrane rigidity from a loss of expression of caveolin-1 and a lower reduction of 15% upon a loss of cavin-1 expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on theoretical modeling using measured parameters and cited values from Raucher and Sheetz, 2000.

claims.claim: There is a significant decrease of 30% of the bending rigidity from κsiCTRL = 23.4 ± 0.9 kBT to κsiCAV1 = 17.0 ± 0.9 kBT.
claims.source: We measured a significant decrease of 30% of the bending rigidity from κsiCTRL = 23.4 ± 0.9 kBT to κsiCAV1 = 17.0 ± 0.9 kBT.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference in bending rigidity in siPTRF conditions compared to siCTRL, with a κsiPTRF = 23.4 ± 1.3 kBT.
claims.source: Moreover, we observed no significant difference in siPTRF conditions compared to siCTRL, with a κsiPTRF = 23.4 ± 1.3 kBT (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The expression of caveolin-1, but not of cavin-1, significantly stiffens the plasma membrane.
claims.source: In good agreement with the theoretical predictions, these measurements establish that the expression of caveolin-1, but not of cavin-1, significantly stiffens the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the membrane tether pulling experiments and theoretical modeling.

claims.claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of key structural and regulatory components of caveolae sensitizes endothelial cells to the formation of TEM tunnels triggered by the inhibition of RhoA-driven actomyosin contractility.
claims.source: We report that siRNA-mediated knockdown of key structural and regulatory components of caveolae sensitizes endothelial cells to the formation of TEM tunnels triggered by the inhibition of RhoA-driven actomyosin contractility.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings from the TEM formation experiments.

claims.claim: Inhibition of RhoA reduces by twofold the pool of caveolae invaginations at the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Hence, inhibition of RhoA reduces by twofold the pool of caveolae invaginations at the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing reduced caveolae density in ExoC3-treated cells.

claims.claim: Targeted depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 caveolae decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which concur to decrease the height of cells favoring membrane apposition for TEM nucleation.
claims.source: Mechanistically, we report that targeted depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 caveolae decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which concur to decrease the height of cells favoring membrane apposition for TEM nucleation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell volume and spreading area measurements shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claims.claim: There is a higher susceptibility of Cav1-deficient mice to lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
claims.source: In good agreement with the recorded increase in TEM formation and width following caveolin-1 knockdown, we establish a higher susceptibility of Cav1-deficient mice to lethal effects triggered by EDIN-B mART during staphylococcal bloodstream infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from mouse infection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: In addition to the well-established role of caveolae in membrane tension homeostasis, caveolin-1 rigidifies plasma membrane either directly or indirectly.
claims.source: Finally, we provide theoretical and experimental evidence that in addition to the well-established role of caveolae in membrane tension homeostasis, caveolin-1 rigidifies plasma membrane either directly or indirectly, as discussed below.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments and theoretical modeling.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%.
claims.source: Our biophysical measurements unravel that caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%, while depletion of cavin-1 has no impact.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Depletion of cavin-1 has no impact on membrane bending rigidity.
claims.source: Our biophysical measurements unravel that caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30%, while depletion of cavin-1 has no impact.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by membrane tether pulling experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The difference between the 30% experimental decrease and 55% theoretical decrease in bending rigidity can be attributed to several approximations in the theoretical model.
claims.source: The difference recorded between these approaches can be attributed to several approximations in the theoretical model, notably the simplified treatment of the physical membrane tension variation, the cytoskeletal contributions, and the interactions between neighboring TEM tunnels.
claims.evidence: This claim is an inference discussing the limitations of the theoretical model.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 is inserted in the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Indeed, since caveolin-1 is inserted in the cytosolic leaflet of the plasma membrane, when a nanotube is pulled toward the exterior of the PMS, we can expect two situations depending on the ability of caveolin-1 to deform membranes, which remains to be addressed (Porta et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Porta et al., 2022 and represents established knowledge about caveolin-1 membrane topology.

claims.claim: A very reduced concentration of Cav1 compared to the plasma membrane has been reported in tunneling nanotubes (TNT) connecting two neighboring cells.
claims.source: Note that the presence of a very reduced concentration of Cav1 compared to the plasma membrane has been reported in tunneling nanotubes (TNT) connecting two neighboring cells (Li et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Previous studies showed that inclusion of integral proteins in membranes had no impact on bending rigidity, as shown in the bacteriorhodopsin experiment.
claims.source: Considering a direct mechanical role of Cav1, previous studies showed that inclusion of integral proteins in membranes had no impact on bending rigidity, as shown in the bacteriorhodopsin experiment (Manneville et al., 1999), or even decreased membrane rigidity as reported for the Ca2+-ATPase SERCA (Girard et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manneville et al., 1999 and Girard et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Previous simulations have confirmed the softening effect of protein inclusions.
claims.source: Previous simulations have also confirmed the softening effect of protein inclusions (Fowler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fowler et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides.
claims.source: Considering an impact on lipid composition, it is well established that caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides (Parton et al., 2020b; Roitenberg et al., 2018), which are known to rigidify membranes (Rawicz et al., 2008; Steinkühler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parton et al., 2020b and Roitenberg et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids are known to rigidify membranes.
claims.source: Considering an impact on lipid composition, it is well established that caveolae are enriched with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, including gangliosides (Parton et al., 2020b; Roitenberg et al., 2018), which are known to rigidify membranes (Rawicz et al., 2008; Steinkühler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rawicz et al., 2008 and Steinkühler et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Caveolin-1 might contribute to the enrichment of the plasma membrane with cholesterol, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids.

results.result: ExoC3 treatment reduces caveolae density at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold (from 5.4 to 3.4 caveolae/µm²), with remaining caveolae evenly distributed and not accumulating around TEM tunnels.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 and C62 are supported by quantitative electron microscopy data (Figure 1B-C) showing reduced caveolae density after ExoC3 treatment. The measurements include appropriate sample sizes (>175 µm² analyzed, n≥16 cells) and statistical analysis showing significant differences.

results.result: Depletion of caveolin-1 or cavin-1 increases TEM formation, with higher percentages of cells displaying TEMs (37.6% siCAV1, 36.4% siPTRF vs 28.8% siCTRL) and increased TEM density per cell (1.96 siCAV1, 1.36 siPTRF vs 0.91 siCTRL).
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C35-C37 are well-supported by quantitative imaging data (Figure 1E, Figure 1—supplement 2A) with large sample sizes (n=1400 cells, 8 experiments) and appropriate statistical analysis (mixed-effect logistic regression, p<0.0001). The inverse correlation between caveolae density and TEM formation is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: siRNA-mediated depletion shows differential effects: siCAV1 reduces both caveolin-1 and cavin-1 by ~80%, while siPTRF leaves ~50% of caveolin-1 unaffected. Neither treatment affects RhoA mono-ADP-ribosylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 are supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1—supplement 1B-C) showing protein levels and RhoA modification status. The differential depletion is important for interpreting subsequent experiments, though the cross-depletion effect of siCAV1 on cavin-1 complicates interpretation of caveolin-1-specific effects.

results.result: ExoC3 treatment induces reorganization of actin cytoskeleton into a loose F-actin meshwork with increased mesh size (~0.2 µm²), with no significant differences between siCTRL, siCAV1, or siPTRF conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 and C77 are supported by 2D STORM imaging data (Figure 2A-B) with appropriate quantification. The finding that caveolin-1 depletion does not exacerbate actin disruption is important for ruling out cytoskeletal mechanisms in the observed TEM phenotypes.

results.result: Caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition synergistically reduce cell height through increased spreading and decreased volume. ExoC3 treatment of siCTRL cells increases spreading by 36% and volume by 17%, resulting in 15% height decrease. siCAV1 and siPTRF treatments further enhance these effects, with siPTRF showing stronger effects on cell shape parameters in the absence of ExoC3.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46, C5, C63, and C80 are supported by quantitative measurements of cell area (Figure 3C), volume (Figure 3D), and calculated height (Table 1) with large sample sizes (n>152-698 cells) and appropriate statistical analysis. The mechanistic link between reduced cell height and increased TEM nucleation is logically sound and supported by the data.

results.result: Caveolin-1 specifically controls TEM opening speed and maximal width. TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1 cells compared to controls, with twofold higher opening speed (2.4 vs 1.1 µm²/s), while time to maximal diameter remains constant across conditions. siPTRF shows minimal effects on these parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C47-C50 are strongly supported by live-cell imaging data (Figure 4B-D) with appropriate temporal resolution (1 frame/second for opening speed measurements). The specific effect of caveolin-1 (but not cavin-1) on TEM dynamics is a key finding, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Cav1-/- mice show increased susceptibility to S. aureus bloodstream infection with catalytically active EDIN-B. At LD50 (2.5×10⁷ CFU/m), Cav1-/- mice had lower survival with WT edinB (11/18 deaths) vs ΔedinB (4/17 deaths, p=0.0123), and catalytically active EDIN-B caused more deaths than inactive mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C52-C55, C64, and C95 are supported by mouse survival experiments (Figure 5) with appropriate group sizes and statistical analysis (Mantel-Cox test). The experiments with catalytically inactive EDIN-B mutant provide important controls establishing causality. However, the direct link to TEM formation in vivo remains inferential.

results.result: Caveolin-1 depletion decreases membrane bending rigidity by 30% (from 23.4±0.9 to 17.0±0.9 kBT) and increases membrane tension twofold, while cavin-1 depletion has no significant effect on bending rigidity. Theoretical modeling predicts 55% reduction in rigidity for siCAV1 and 15% for siPTRF.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C56-C60, C65-C67, C78, and C91 are supported by membrane tether pulling experiments (Figure 6D) and theoretical modeling. The experimental measurements show clear differences with non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals for siCAV1 vs siCTRL. The discrepancy between experimental (30%) and theoretical (55%) predictions is acknowledged and attributed to model approximations (C68).

results.result: The difference between experimental (30%) and theoretical (55%) decreases in bending rigidity can be attributed to approximations in the theoretical model, including simplified treatment of membrane tension variation, cytoskeletal contributions, and TEM interactions.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 provides a reasonable explanation for the quantitative discrepancy between theory and experiment. The authors appropriately acknowledge model limitations, though this suggests the theoretical framework may need refinement.

results.result: Membrane tension and bending rigidity are the minimal mechanical parameters determining TEM nucleation and maximal size. Membrane tension drives TEM nucleation and initial opening speed, while bending rigidity sets maximal TEM aperture size. The minimal precursor tunnel size increases with bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C22, C79, and C87 are supported by the combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurements. The physical model (Equations 1-6) provides a framework consistent with the experimental observations, though some assumptions (e.g., limited cytoskeletal contribution) may be oversimplified.

results.result: The mechanisms by which caveolin-1 and cavin-1 regulate TEM nucleation differ: both reduce cell height favoring membrane apposition, but only caveolin-1 depletion increases membrane tension and decreases bending rigidity, further favoring TEM nucleation by decreasing the required minimal precursor tunnel radius.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 integrate multiple experimental findings into a coherent mechanistic model. The differential effects of caveolin-1 vs cavin-1 on membrane mechanics provide a clear explanation for their distinct impacts on TEM dynamics.

results.result: Caveolin-1 might contribute to plasma membrane enrichment with rigidifying lipids (cholesterol, sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids), and caveolae depletion with RhoA inactivation may release membrane-folding-driven mechanical constraints limiting cell spreading.
results.evaluation: Claims C75 and C85 are explicitly speculative ("might contribute," "may release"). While plausible based on known caveolae lipid composition (C73-C74), these mechanisms lack direct experimental support in this study. Further experiments are needed to test these hypotheses.

results.result: Discussion of potential mechanisms for caveolin-1's effect on membrane rigidity, including its membrane topology, reduced concentration in tunneling nanotubes, effects of protein inclusions on membrane rigidity, and enrichment of rigidifying lipids in caveolae.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 and C76 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These provide context for interpreting the experimental findings, though they don't directly test mechanisms in this study.

results.result: Cell volume regulation during spreading: ExoC3-triggered spreading occurs with decreased cell volume, and caveolae depletion decreases cell volume independently of RhoA signaling. This is consistent with known mechanisms of cell volume homeostasis during spreading.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by cell volume measurements (Figure 3D) and appropriate citations. The finding that caveolae control volume independently of RhoA is novel, though the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Caveolin-1 expression has bidirectional effects on S. aureus susceptibility: OTULIN haploinsufficiency increases caveolin-1 levels, sensitizing cells to α-hemolysin, while caveolin-1 loss sensitizes to EDIN-B. Caveolin-1 expression is not regulated by RhoA signaling. EDIN-B is associated with hemoptysis in S. aureus pneumonia patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94, C96, and C99 are supported by appropriate citations (C92-C93, C96) and experimental data (C94: Figure 1—supplement 1A). The bidirectional effects highlight the complexity of caveolin-1's role in host-pathogen interactions, though the clinical relevance of TEMs remains to be established.

results.result: Background knowledge on endothelial barrier function, bacterial mART exotoxins, TEM formation mechanisms, caveolae structure and function, and effects of RhoA inhibition on vascular permeability.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C29, C97-C98 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Summary statement: siRNA-mediated knockdown of caveolae components sensitizes endothelial cells to TEM formation triggered by RhoA inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 accurately summarizes the main experimental findings supported by multiple lines of evidence throughout the manuscript.

results.result: TEM nucleation requires apposition of basal and apical membranes, which is hindered by intermembrane distance (cell height).
results.evaluation: Claim C86 represents a fundamental physical principle underlying TEM formation, supported by the experimental observations linking cell height to TEM frequency.

results.result: Depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 increases TEM formation frequency. siRNA-mediated knockdown of caveolin-1 (siCAV1) and cavin-1 (siPTRF) both increase the percentage of cells displaying TEMs and the density of TEMs per cell. RhoA inhibition by ExoC3 reduces caveolae density at the plasma membrane by 1.6-fold, and the remaining caveolae are evenly distributed without accumulation around TEMs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'This important study identifies the role of caveolin-1 and cavin1 as regulators of transendothelial macroaperture (TEM)' and describe the work as 'rigorous and compelling.' The reviewer notes 'the accumulation of pieces of evidence collected from each type of approach makes very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors.'

results.result: Caveolae depletion and RhoA inhibition synergistically reduce cell height to favor TEM nucleation. Depletion of caveolin-1 and cavin-1 decreases cell volume and increases cell spreading, which together reduce cell height. This reduction in cell height, combined with disruption of the F-actin meshwork by RhoA inhibition, favors membrane apposition required for TEM nucleation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. The reviewer specifically praises the 'quality of STORM images (Fig. 2) which are very illuminating and useful, in particular for validating some hypotheses of the theoretical analysis,' directly supporting the actin meshwork observations. The comprehensive nature of the work is noted as making the conclusions 'very convincing.'

results.result: Caveolin-1 specifically controls TEM opening speed and maximal width. TEMs are 5.4-fold wider in siCAV1-treated cells compared to controls, with a twofold higher opening speed (2.4 µm²/s vs 1.1 µm²/s). In contrast, cavin-1 depletion has only minor effects on TEM opening dynamics, while the time to reach maximal diameter remains identical across all conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this as a key finding, stating the work 'pins down the key role of caveolin-1' and noting that the evidence makes 'very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors on the new role of cavolin-1 as an individual protein instead of the main molecular component of caveolae.' The distinction between caveolin-1 and cavin-1 effects is implicitly accepted through the overall positive assessment.

results.result: Caveolin-1 deficiency sensitizes mice to lethal effects of EDIN-B during S. aureus bloodstream infection. CAV1 KO mice show significantly higher lethality when infected with S. aureus producing catalytically active EDIN-B compared to the inactive mutant or deletion strain. This establishes that caveolin-1 expression confers resistance to EDIN-B mART pathogenicity during septicemia.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this in vivo validation, describing the work as 'comprehensive' with 'in vitro work based on siRNA knockdown and optical imaging approach complemented with an in vivo work on mice.' The multi-faceted approach including mouse experiments is noted as contributing to the 'very convincing' nature of the conclusions.

results.result: Caveolin-1 specifically increases membrane bending rigidity independent of caveolae. Membrane tether pulling experiments show caveolin-1 depletion decreases bending rigidity by 30% (from 23.4 to 17.0 kBT), while cavin-1 depletion has no effect. Theoretical modeling predicts a 55% reduction, with the difference attributed to model approximations. Caveolin-1 depletion also increases membrane tension twofold, while cavin-1 depletion affects neither tension nor rigidity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding, stating 'the accumulation of pieces of evidence collected from each type of approach makes very convincing the conclusion drawn by the authors on the new role of cavolin-1 as an individual protein.' The biophysical measurements are part of the 'rigorous' methodology that is 'compelling.' The theoretical modeling is discussed positively below.

results.result: Membrane tension and bending rigidity are the minimal mechanical parameters determining TEM nucleation and maximal size. The theoretical model based on dewetting processes predicts that membrane rigidity sets maximal TEM aperture size, and that the minimal precursor tunnel size increases with bending rigidity and decreases with membrane tension. The model shows reasonable agreement with experimental measurements despite some approximations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly validate the theoretical approach, stating 'The analogy with dewetting processes drawn to derive the theoretical model is very attractive' and noting that 'the STORM analysis...show that HUVECs intoxicated by ExoC3 exhibit a loose and defective cortex with a significantly increase mesh size, which supports this hypothesis.' The reviewer acknowledges that 'the validity of the Helfrich formalism is a key assumption' but accepts it is now supported by the STORM data.

results.result: The mechanism by which caveolin-1 increases membrane rigidity remains uncertain. The authors discuss several hypotheses including direct mechanical effects of caveolin-1 insertion, indirect effects through lipid composition changes (cholesterol, sphingomyelin, glycosphingolipids enrichment), but acknowledge the exact mechanism requires further investigation. Previous studies suggest protein inclusions typically soften rather than stiffen membranes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this limitation, stating 'While this work pins down the key role of caveolin-1, its mechanism remains to be further investigated' and 'Even though we may feel slightly frustrated by the absence of data in this direction, the quality and merit of this paper remain.' The hypotheses are described as 'very plausible though challenging.'

results.result: Background and contextual claims about endothelial barrier function, bacterial toxins, caveolae structure, and related literature. These claims establish the scientific context including: mART exotoxins compromise endothelial barriers by inhibiting RhoA; caveolae are mechano-regulators that buffer membrane tension; caveolin-1 and RhoA crosstalk is important for endothelial mechanosensing; and variations in caveolin-1 expression have bidirectional impacts on S. aureus susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these background claims, which are well-supported by citations and represent established knowledge in the field. The reviewers focus their evaluation on the novel experimental findings rather than the contextual framework.
